2027-07-17.title: Second Saturday of Kaitha
2027-07-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God chose the poor to be heirs of the kingdom
Those who eat the bread of heaven are blessed: the great dinner
2027-07-17.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which follows the Season of the Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when we remember the apostles, martyrs and saints who sowed the Gospel and watered it with their blood, and keep ourselves ready for the coming of the Lord. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “God selected the poor as the heirs of heaven”; “Those who eat the bread of heaven are blessed”.
2027-07-17.verse: And the slave said, “Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.”
theo: Saturday in the second week of Kaitha puts before us two tables: the assembly of the Church in James, and the banquet of the kingdom in Luke. James begins with a question that cuts: “My brothers and sisters, do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?” His picture is simple and true to life. “If a person with gold rings and in fine clothes comes into your assembly, and if a poor person in dirty clothes also comes in, and if you take notice of the one wearing the fine clothes and say, ‘Have a seat here, please,’ while to the one who is poor you say, ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit at my feet,’ have you not made distinctions among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?” The assembly of the Church, which gathers around the Lord's table, is the one place where no one should be placed by his clothes or his wallet. In our own parishes, at the feast-day lunch and at the Sunday Qurbana, the question is just as real: who is welcomed first, who is asked to speak, who is given the good seat, and who stands at the back?

James then says what God does: “Listen, my beloved brothers and sisters. Has not God chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith and to be heirs of the kingdom that he has promised to those who love him?” God does not despise the rich; but he has a special tenderness for the poor, and the Church's teaching speaks of a preferential love for them. James reminds a community in trouble that the very people they flatter are often those who drag them into court, and “you have dishonored the poor.” The remedy is what he calls the royal law, the law of the King: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Moses had already forbidden partiality in a court: “you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great: with justice you shall judge your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:15). Whoever loves in this way does well; whoever flatters the great and scorns the small breaks the law of love, however religious he may seem.

In Luke's Gospel Jesus is a guest at table in the house of a leading Pharisee. One of the guests, hearing him talk of invitations and of the resurrection, says a pious thing: “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” Jesus answers with a story. “Someone gave a great dinner and invited many. At the time for the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come; for everything is ready now.’ But they all alike began to make excuses.” The excuses are polite, and the things they name are good things: “I have bought a piece of land, and I must go out and see it”; “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out”; “I have just been married, and therefore I cannot come.” Land, work and family are not evil. But each guest puts a good thing before the invitation, and the host's “everything is ready now” goes unanswered. Saint Gregory the Great read in these three excuses the land of pride and possession, the oxen of busy affairs, and the wife of comfort; whatever the reading, the lesson is that the call of God cannot always wait until our business is finished.

Then the host's anger turns into a welcome. “Go out at once into the streets and lanes of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.” The slave goes, and comes back: “Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.” There is still room: it is the sentence that has driven the Church's mission since the first apostles. The master sends him again to the roads and lanes, “and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.” The word “compel” is not an order to force anyone, for the faith can never be forced; it is the host's insistent, urgent love that will not take a polite refusal from those who have never been asked. The parable is not a verdict on any people: it is a mirror held up to each of us who has heard the call, and has found a reason to wait. Put James and Luke together: the poor in the assembly are the guests of the banquet, and the one who prefers the well-dressed to the stranger has already found his excuse. Where is the Qurbana's table set? In the middle of the street, with room for one more. In the Season of Kaitha, the season of harvest, the Church prays that the house will be filled.
outline: Two tables: the assembly in James and the great dinner in Luke.
Gold rings and dirty clothes; the royal law of love; the one place where no one is ranked by his wallet.
Rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom; the preferential love of the Church.
The excuses of the invited: good things before the call.
The streets and lanes; the host's urgent love; the house that must be filled.
“Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.”
live: At the next Qurbana or parish gathering, greet first and sit beside someone whom nobody is sitting with: a newcomer, an old person, someone poor.
Look at the excuse you most often give God: work, property, family business. Set aside one hour this week to answer his invitation: the Qurbana, a prayer, a visit.
fathers: Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not despise him when he is naked. Do not honour him here in church with silk vestments, and then neglect him outside, where he is cold and naked.

The three excuses are three snares of the world: the land stands for the pride of possession, the oxen for the care of earthly business, and the wife for the pleasures of the flesh. Whoever is held by them does not come to the banquet.
The Lord did not forbid the rich to be saved; he asked that wealth be made a servant and not a master, and that it be used to feed, to clothe and to welcome the needy.
magis: God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor and rebukes those who turn away from them: “Give to him who begs from you, do not refuse him who would borrow from you”.
The love of the Church for the poor is part of her constant tradition, inspired by the Gospel of the Beatitudes and by the poverty of Jesus.
The Lord addresses an invitation to us, urging us to receive him in the sacrament of the Eucharist.
saints: 13–18 July: the second week of Kaitha. Tue 13 and Wed 14: Second Tuesday and Wednesday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta, an Ordinary Feast of the Oriental tradition (in the Latin calendar, St Bonaventure). Fri 16: the Second Friday of Kaitha, Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai, and Our Lady of Mount Carmel, an Important Marian Feast. Sat 17: Second Saturday of Kaitha. Sun 18: Third Sunday of Kaitha. Looking ahead: St Mary Magdalene on Thursday 22 July, and St Alphonsa, the first woman of India to be raised to the altars, on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, host of the great supper, you invite us and tell us that everything is ready. Forgive us the excuses we have put before your call, and the favouritism we have shown in your house. Teach us to love our neighbour as ourselves; make us glad to see the poor in your Church, and give us a heart that makes room for one more. Fill your house with those who have never been asked, and bring us all to the table of your kingdom, where you live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord sets his table and says, “Come; for everything is ready now.” The bread of heaven is given in the same way to the rich man and the beggar, the old and the child, the stranger and the neighbour. Whoever comes to this altar and then despises his brother has not understood the supper: we come as guests, and the master has room for one more.

quick: James: favouritism toward the rich in the assembly breaks the royal law of love; God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom.
Luke: the great dinner; the invited make excuses; the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame are brought in; “there is still room”.
Together: God's table is open to all, and his invitation cannot wait on our business.
2027-07-17.action: Greet and sit beside a person at the next parish gathering whom others overlook.
2027-07-17.question: What excuse do I give when God says, “Come; everything is ready now”?

family.explain: Once a man made a big dinner and invited many friends. But when he said, “Come, everything is ready,” they all made excuses: one had to see his new field, one had to try his new oxen, one had just been married. The man was sad, and he said to his servant, “Go to the streets and invite the poor and the lame and the blind!” And the servant said, “There is still room.” That is how God is: he asks everybody to his house, and he loves those whom nobody invites. We can do the same: we can invite the child who sits alone, the old neighbour, the family that has little.
family.intention: We pray for the poor, the lonely and the stranger, and for the house of God to be full.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom shall we invite to our table this week, someone who cannot invite us back?”

illus: At a parish feast near Kanjirappally (a story told to illustrate the reading) the council had put up two long tables in the hall for the feast-day lunch, with a smaller table for the guests of honour. At the gate stood an old man in a torn shirt, a scrap collector named Velu, who had come to ask for some water. A young trustee saw him and looked at the hall. ‘There is no room,’ he started to say, and then he stopped, because the vicar had been preaching that morning on the great dinner. He picked up his plate from the guests' table, went to the gate and said, ‘Velu chettan, there is still room. Please sit here.’ The old man shook his head, laughing; but when he was seated, an elderly widow passed him the rice without a word, and the lady next to her filled his glass. The vicar later told the story at the next Sunday Qurbana, and wrote on the notice-board in his own hand: ‘There is still room.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you invite everyone to the supper of your kingdom. Gather us in the same assembly, rich and poor together, and open our hearts to hear your call without delay. Amen.
share: Do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ? (James 2:1). Whom do I treat better, and whom do I overlook?
Has not God chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith? (James 2:5). What have the poor taught me about faith?
They all alike began to make excuses (Luke 14:18). Which good thing have I put before God's call?
There is still room (Luke 14:22). Whom can I bring to the Lord's table?
pm.resp: Lord, make room in our hearts for all.
interc: For the poor, the lonely and the strangers in our parishes, that they may be welcomed first at the table of the Church.
For priests and parish councils, that they may keep the doors of the Church open to all without favouritism.
For those who put work, wealth or family before God's call, that they may answer his invitation.
For those who have never heard the Gospel and for all who are still outside the house, that the Lord may fill it.
For ourselves, that we may love our neighbour as ourselves.
pm.close: Father, you prepare a table for all peoples and you ask us to make room. Make us welcoming in your house and ready to answer your call. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today the readings put two tables before us. In the first, James asks: “Do you with your acts of favoritism really believe in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ?” (James 2:1). A person with gold rings comes into the assembly, and we give him the best seat. A poor person in dirty clothes comes in, and we say, “Stand there.”

James says: this is not the Lord's way. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). The law that rules the Christian assembly is the royal law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (James 2:8). In our churches nobody should be placed higher or lower because of his clothes or his money.

In the Gospel, Jesus tells of a man who gave a great dinner and invited many. “Come; for everything is ready now.” But they all made excuses (Luke 14:17–18): a field, oxen, a wedding. These are all good things. But when God calls, they cannot be put first.

Then the master sends his servant to the streets and lanes to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame. The servant says, “there is still room” (Luke 14:22). That is the heart of God: there is always room for one more. We should be the same.

This week let us look at our excuses, and let us look at the person nobody notices. Let us greet that person, sit with him, and invite him. And let us answer the Lord's call: “Come; for everything is ready now.” Amen.
kids: Children, God invited everybody to a great feast, even those whom nobody invited. When someone is alone at school or in the church, you can say, “Come and sit with us. There is still room!”

At the time for the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come; for everything is ready now.’
points.apply: Name your usual excuse and set aside one hour this week for God.

q: The rich and the poor have this in common: the Lord is the maker of them all.
And the slave said, “Sir, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.”
points.apply: Invite someone who cannot invite you back to your table or your church.

concl: The Church's table is the Lord's table: no favourites, a place for the poor, and room for one more.
Let us answer the call without excuse and make room for those who have not been asked.
2027-07-17.resolve: This week, greet someone nobody sits with, invite someone who cannot repay you, and set aside an hour to answer God's call.
